newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean opposition links president to scandal.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean opposition links president to scandal.

text.p: South Korea's main opposition party opened an election year offensive on Wednesday by charging President Kim Young-sam used money from scandal-ridden Hanbo Group to fund his campaign for office.
The National Congress for National Politics alleged Hanbo contributed 60 billion won ($67 million) to help finance Kim's 1992 presidential campaign.
A statement also charged that Kim dipped into a slush fund amassed by his disgraced predecessor Roh Tae-woo, now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.
"The prosecution should immediately open a probe into the presidential election fund," it said.
"President Kim Young-sam should reveal how he raised and spent one trillion won, including 300 billion won from Roh Tae-woo and 60 billion won from Hanbo," it said.

Financing of the 1992 vote is potentially one of the most explosive issues in presidential elections set for December, as is a loans-for-kickbacks scandal swirling around Hanbo's failed steelmaking unit.
By linking the two, the opposition is preparing a gloves-off contest for the December vote.
Kim has fudged the campaign financing issue in the past, saying he had no direct hand in fund-raising.
Under South Korean election law, his campaign spending limit was legally set at 36.7 billion won, although his ruling party has reported that the amount spent was far less -- 28.4 billion won.
"The core of the scandal lies in the election fund," National Congress spokeswoman Park Sun-suck told Reuters. "Loans were provided to Hanbo in return for Hanbo's contribution to the campaign."

The accusation came as state prosecutors arrested close associates of the president's second son, Kim Hyun-chul, on charges that they took bribes in return for promises to lobby the younger Kim for favours.
"We have secured arrest warrants from a criminal court against Mr Kim Hi-chan and Mr Park Tae-joong and put them into custody," a prosecution official said.
Prosecutors charged the two took kickbacks from businessmen on promises that they would ask the president's son to help them obtain government licences for broadcasting and other projects.

The prosecution official, who asked not to be identified, said prosecutors had secured evidence implicating Kim Hyun-chul in offences unrelated to Hanbo. An arrest warrant would be sought by the end of next week.
A prosecution spokesman said on Tuesday an investigation found no evidence linking Kim Hyun-chul with the scandal over Hanbo Steel Co, which collapsed in January under $5.8 billion in debts.
"The prosecution is trying to issue a document of acquittal to Kim Hyun-chul over his role in the scandal by arresting him for 'personal irregularities'," the National Congress spokeswoman said.
During parliamentary hearings this month, opposition lawmakers accused the junior Kim of peddling influence to keep loans rolling in to Hanbo Steel.
Kim Hyun-chul, who played a key role in his father's 1992 election campaign, denied the charges.
The National Congress statement denounced Kim's ruling New Korea Party and his presidential office of plotting to cover up funds used during his 1992 election campaign.
